Crude Oil Surpasses $100 Following Middle East Deployments
Global crude oil benchmarks surged past 100 dollars a barrel on October 1, driven by rising military tensions in the Middle East and new export curbs imposed by Chinese refiners, hani.co.kr reported. The convergence of tightening fuel supplies and escalating geopolitical conflict prompted analysts to adjust ongoing price forecasts upward across international markets.
Brent Crude Climbs Past One Hundred Dollars Following Middle East Deployments
New front-month Brent crude futures for December settlement rose 4.28 dollars, or 4.37 percent, to close at 102.31 dollars per barrel on October 1. American West Texas Intermediate (WTI) futures gained 2.45 dollars, or 2.71 percent, ending the session at 92.87 dollars per barrel. The price increases erased earlier losses after markets absorbed word of fresh supply restrictions originating from major Asian consumers.
United States President Donald Trump stated on October 1 that his administration is weighing renewed military options against Iran following the November midterm elections. Washington is currently dispatching a third aircraft carrier and up to 10,000 additional troops to the Middle East. Speaking to reporters at the White House before departing for campaign events, Trump said a decision must be reached soon, adding that Iran must sign a fair agreement or face severe consequences.
Chinese Fuel Export Ban Raises Crude Price Concerns
The military maneuvers coincided with reports that Chinese refiners have suspended exports of petroleum products to all destinations outside Hong Kong and Macau until further notice. Crude prices reversed an initial one-percent drop during the trading session immediately following the announcement of the export halt. Giovanni Staunovo, an analyst at UBS, told Reuters that the export ban reflects domestic anxieties over local petroleum supply stability. Staunovo noted that it is unclear whether the measure will ultimately trigger expanded crude imports following recent declines in domestic reserves.
Refining infrastructure damage across the Gulf region and Russia has sustained a prolonged shortage of diesel and other refined products. Vladimir Putin stated that Russia will withhold diesel shipments from global energy markets until international sanctions against Moscow are lifted. Russia’s ongoing export ban through October has left worldwide diesel inventories severely constrained, with industry participants anticipating that the supply deficit will persist into next year. The European Union energy task force scheduled a meeting for October 2 to discuss potential releases from emergency diesel stockpiles. Meanwhile, the Trump administration notified Germany and France that they face potential restrictions on American diesel exports if they fail to deploy emergency reserves.
Shipping Disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and Evolving Price Forecasts
Maritime security risks intensified in the Strait of Hormuz as physical transit routes faced active threats. Marine risk data service Mariske reported on September 30 that three Liberian-flagged tankers transiting the strait sustained hits from unidentified projectiles. Regional sources indicate that Tehran is preparing expansive defensive measures in the event of large-scale American military interventions.
Compensating flows have emerged from other parts of the region as Saudi Arabia resumed tanker loadings at Yanbu along the Red Sea coast following the restart of its East-West pipeline. Goldman Sachs estimated in a September 29 report that Gulf petroleum exports—including vessels operating with transponders disabled—doubled through September, returning to average 2025 volumes at 23.3 million barrels per day during the final week of the month. Sustained market disruptions have nonetheless driven analysts to revise their average 2026 Brent price projections upward to 89.05 dollars per barrel.
